sections.heading: Is Silicone Roof Coating Better Than Elastomeric?

c.v: Silicone is itself an elastomeric coating, so the real comparison is silicone vs. acrylic vs. polyurethane.

runs.v: Silicone coatings offer the best ponding water resistance and UV protection of the three: a high-solids white silicone reflects roughly 80% to 90% of sunlight when new, and because it reflects heat, a reflective white silicone coating can lower roof surface temperatures by more than 50°F, per the DOE. Silicone cures with atmospheric moisture into a film that resists permanent standing water, resists mold and mildew, and stays flexible through temperature shifts, which makes silicone systems ideal for flat roofs with drainage issues, backed by proven performance on ponding decks. Acrylic's water based formula is the cost effective choice for a roof that drains and stays cleaner, and it accepts an acrylic recoat, while polyurethane is the toughest against foot traffic and impact, and its aromatic grades need a UV-stable top coat. On a flat roof that ponds, a silicone roof coating is usually the better choice; on a draining roof, acrylic can be.

sections.heading: Rain, Freeze-Thaw, and Application Weather in Montclair

runs.v: Montclair experiences significant rainfall and harsh winter conditions, so the weather sets the application window. Silicone coatings require specific ambient and surface temperature conditions for application: the roof surface has to be dry and commonly at least 5°F above the dew point, acrylic needs temperatures near 50°F and rising plus dry hours to cure, and moisture-cure silicone can go on in cooler, more humid weather within the maker's limits. Overcast skies are fine as long as no rain is forecast before the film skins over, and a cured silicone film stays flexible through freeze-thaw cycles.

sections.heading: What Are the Downsides of Using Silicone Roof Coating?

runs.v: Silicone costs more per square foot than acrylic, holds dirt so its reflectance drops faster, is slippery when wet, and accepts only silicone for future recoats; acrylic re-emulsifies under ponding water; and aromatic polyurethane chalks in sunlight without a top coat. faqs.q: Should I choose a silicone or an acrylic elastomeric coating for my Montclair roof?

runs.v: Choose silicone over acrylic when ponding or standing water lingers on the roof, and acrylic over silicone when dirt-pickup and recoatability matter, because acrylic re-washes cleaner with rainfall while silicone holds dirt and loses reflectance faster, per the RCMA and coating manufacturers.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to coat a commercial or multi-family roof in Montclair?

runs.v: A recoat on a detached one- or two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and needs no construction permit, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code. On a commercial, multi-family, or attached building, a roofing overhaul typically requires a construction permit, and repairing more than 25% of the roof area in 12 months triggers one, with recover-versus-tear-off limits under N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4, so confirm with the Montclair construction office before work.
